title: Progressive degradation messaging and competitive anchors
body:
Purpose:
This doc collects candidate language, competitive framing, and short incident narrative templates for talking about Redwood’s approach to graceful degradation, fallbacks, and multi-region failover. It’s intended for sales, solutions, CS, and comms to use when explaining risk tradeoffs and operational guarantees to engineering and product stakeholders at prospects and customers.

Context / problem statement:
Customers want two things that are often at odds: uninterrupted user experiences and predictable unit economics. When an LLM service faces capacity constraints, network incidents, or model regressions, naive messaging either overpromises (causes trust loss when failure occurs) or over-technicalizes (confuses non-engineering stakeholders). We need a consistent set of plain-language narratives and competitive anchors that: (1) explain how Redwood degrades, (2) show how we prioritize user-facing continuity, and (3) highlight where Redwood’s model routing, caching and regional architecture reduce customer impact relative to alternatives.

High-level positioning statements (elevator variants):
- For engineering leaders: "Redwood keeps your features responsive by degrading features intentionally — we route, cache, and fall back to compatible model variants so your front-end stays healthy while costs stay predictable."
- For product/PMs: "When demand or capacity changes, Redwood gracefully reduces model fidelity in controlled steps rather than abruptly dropping service — preserving user flows and metrics that matter to your business."
- For executives/security: "Redwood’s multi-tiered fallback plan and regional redundancy mean continued availability with auditable decision paths and clear escalation commitments."

Core messaging pillars (short):
1) Predictable degradation: explicit, tiered fallback modes (quality-preserving variant, latency-first variant, degraded feature) that are configurable by route.
2) Observable & reversible: telemetry, canary rollouts, and automated regressions alerts tied to prompt tests so customers can see the impact in near real-time.
3) Economically sensible: fallbacks are designed to reduce per-token cost while limiting user-visible regressions.
4) Continuity-first architecture: multi-region routing + peer cache + prefix/KV cache preserve in-flight sessions and reduce cold-start regressions.

Fallback taxonomy (recommended public-friendly phrasing):
- Variant fallback: "Switch to a compatible model variant with lower compute needs but similar behavior" (good for short capacity spikes).
- Response-thinning: "Trim optional content (summaries, long-form elaboration) while keeping core answers intact" (used for latency SLO preservation).
- Feature-shed: "Temporarily disable non-essential features (advanced hallucination filters, long-context memory) with clear client-side flags" (used for sustained capacity constraints).
- Regional routing: "Redirect traffic to a healthy region, with data locality and compliance options honored" (used for regional outages).
- Queue/backpressure with graceful decline: "Provide a near-instant client signal that a request is delayed or degraded and surface options (retry, lower fidelity, offline fallback)".

How to present fallbacks to customers (templates):
- Short public status message (external): "We’re experiencing partial service constraints and are routing requests to reduce latency; most features remain available with slightly reduced response length. No action required on your side."
- Support-facing explanation (CS to technical contact): "We proactively routed traffic to a compatible lower-latency model variant and enabled prefix caching for your busiest endpoints — this reduced tail latency by ~40% while keeping API shape identical. We can pause the fallback or adjust thresholds for your Dedicated capacity plan."
- Executive summary (for CSM/AM to buyer execs): "Our multi-tier fallbacks prioritize your most important calls. During the incident, core product flows stayed online with minor quality changes; we’ll share a post-incident evaluation and tuning plan tied to your top prompt lists."

Incident narrative templates (role-specific snippets):
- For Sales during contract review: "We map your critical routes to explicit SLOs and can document per-route fallback policies in the contract (e.g., ‘route A: always maintain >95% confidence, route B: allow latency-first fallback’). That gives you clear operational guarantees and a playbook we’ll execute if capacity is constrained."
- For SRE/ops during incident comms: "Timeline: detection -> automatic model variant failover -> prefix cache warming -> monitoring shows recovery. Impact: X% of requests saw shortened responses for 12 minutes. Mitigations: throttles relaxed, cooldown, and rollback window opened. Next steps: postmortem and threshold tuning."
- For CS/AM to upset user: "We understand the experience differed from normal. Our system took a conservative approach to keep your application live while reducing per-token compute. We’ve prioritized collecting the prompt samples that were affected so we can fine-tune your fallback thresholds."

Competitive framing (quick notes):
- Versus large cloud vendor managed endpoints: "They offer regional endpoints but often default to simple fail-open or queueing behavior; Redwood exposes configurable, per-route fallback policies and active model-variant routing that limit user-visible regression while controlling cost."
- Versus simplicity-first LLM APIs: "Some competitors choose latency or access simplicity over deterministic degradation. We trade off intentionally — you get clear, auditable degradation modes rather than unpredictable slowdowns or opaque errors."
- Versus inference-only infra vendors: "Self-hosted runtimes can be tuned, but customers bear the ops burden. Redwood combines a production-hardened runtime with policy controls, observability, and fallbacks as a managed layer so customers don’t build robust degradation logic themselves."

Trust signals to surface (what to show customers):
- Per-route historical degrade reports (show frequency, duration, and user-impacted metrics).
- Canary test results and prompt set regressions (before/after examples).
- Decision audit logs: when and why a fallback triggered (automatic vs manual).
- Runbook excerpt in the contract: SLO tiers, escalation timelines, and rollout windows.

Example customer-facing scripts (short):
- Outbound post-incident email subject: "Update on recent service disruption — what we did and how we’re improving"
  Body bullets: Detection time, customer impact summary, immediate mitigations (variant routing, cache), measurable outcome (latency or error reduction), next steps (postmortem ETA, action items).

FAQ (sales/CS one-liners):
- Q: "Will fallback change my API surface?" A: "No — fallbacks preserve the API schema; only the model variant or response length changes."
- Q: "Can we disable fallbacks for a specific route?" A: "Yes — per-route policies can pin versions and disable automatic fallbacks; we advise pinned routes paired with Dedicated capacity."
- Q: "Is data routed across regions during failover?" A: "By default we honor your data locality settings; regional failover options are explicit and auditable."

Action items / next deliverables (short):
- Draft a 1-pager for AEs that lists per-plan fallback behavior (due: 2026-03-01) — owner: Diego.
- Create a short demo script for Solutions that shows a live fallback and rollback (due: 2026-02-28) — owner: Avery.
- Add a collapsible section to the Console UI with recent fallback events and rationale (product ticket: JIRA-9821).

Open questions / tradeoffs we’re still hashing:
- How prescriptive should contract-level fallback controls be vs. providing defaults? (legal/commercial impacts).
- How to quantify "user-visible quality" consistently across customers? Need a small common prompt set or metric baseline per vertical.

Useful references and context links:
- Existing go-to-market playbooks in drive (see related docs in this folder).
- CONFLUENCE-6789: fallback policy design notes.
- JIRA-9821: console UI fallback history feature.
- Slack:#infra-ops thread 2025-10-22: notes from the last multi-region DR test.

Notes to self (working):
- Keep language non-technical for execs but give a clear escalation path for engineers.
- Collect two or three real customer examples we can anonymize and include in the one-pager.
- Validate competitor statements with field intel (Sales to confirm).

End.
